title: JSON helpers, validation, problem-details errors (RFC 9457)
summary: Decode request bodies strictly (size cap, unknown fields, one value), validate business rules at the edge, and answer failures as application/problem+json. Go 1.27's encoding/json/v2 makes the strict part the default.

examples.title: A strict decode helper and what each bad body gets back

annotations.note: MaxBytesReader caps what the server will read. Past the limit, Read returns *http.MaxBytesError, and a real server also closes the connection after the response, so a client can't stream gigabytes into a JSON endpoint. A plain io.LimitReader would just truncate and look like malformed JSON.

By default encoding/json ignores keys it doesn't know, so a client's typo ("agee") silently becomes the zero value. Rejecting unknown fields turns that into a 400 the client developer sees immediately.
Decode reads one value and stops; the rest of the body is never looked at. A second Decode must hit io.EOF, otherwise the body held more than one value. Trailing whitespace is fine.

The one place decode errors become statuses. Messages are written for the client: the raw UnmarshalTypeError text names Go structs and types, an internal detail. A body over the limit is 413, not 400. The remaining errors describe only the client's own input, so they pass through. errors.As fits a switch; errors.AsType returns two values and doesn't.
The handler states intent; the helpers carry the rules. Every endpoint that takes JSON calls the same two functions, so the API rejects bad input the same way everywhere.

null decodes without error and leaves the struct at its zero value ("hello  (0)"). Decoding proves the syntax, not the content: that is what validation in example 3 is for. Strict v1 also accepts duplicate and differently cased keys; example 2 shows why that matters and what v2 does instead.

A ResponseRecorder calls the handler directly, with no server and no socket; the decode errors are the same ones a real server would see. Lesson go.http.cors-cookies-httptest covers this way of testing.
This is the hardened v1 decoder from example 1, still the most common form in existing code, including StackLab's own run handler.
UnmarshalRead consumes the whole reader and requires exactly one value, so the trailing-data check comes built in. RejectUnknownMembers is the v2 spelling of DisallowUnknownFields.

v2 picks "cannot" or "unable to" for a SemanticError's message at random, once per process, so that nobody matches on the text. Branch on errors.Is(err, json.ErrUnknownName) or on the error's fields; JSONPointer says where in the body the problem is.

A parser differential: a proxy that reads the first "name" and a Go service that reads the last one disagree about who the request is for. v2 rejects duplicate names and matches names case-sensitively.

A client that sends Windows-1254 (or ISO-8859-9) instead of UTF-8 turns ş into byte 0xFE. v1 replaces it with U+FFFD and stores "Ay�e" for good; v2 rejects the body, so the client learns about its encoding bug at once.

examples.title: Validation at the edge, answered as problem details

annotations.note: RFC 9457 defines type, title, status, detail and instance, and allows extension members; clients must ignore members they don't know. The errors array with pointer and detail follows the RFC's own validation example.

Rules that types can't express live in one method. All failures are collected rather than returned at the first one. "Gülşen Çağlayıcı" is 16 characters but 22 bytes: a len(name) > 20 check would have rejected a valid name. PostgreSQL's varchar(20) counts characters too.
mail.ParseAddress also accepts "Name <addr>" forms, so the parsed address must equal the input. Format checks stop here; whether the mailbox exists is a confirmation e-mail's job, not a regex's.

The Content-Type header is set before WriteHeader, because headers set afterwards are dropped. Problems get application/problem+json, so a client can tell an error body from a resource without looking at the status first. Taking the status from p itself keeps the status member and the real response status from disagreeing.
With type "about:blank" the problem means no more than its status code, and the RFC says title should then be the status phrase. StackLab's httpapi.problem function writes this form for every error.

422: the JSON was well-formed but the content breaks the rules. 400 stays for bodies that can't be parsed. A custom type URI names the kind of problem, and clients switch on type, never on title or detail text.

use_cases: Every JSON endpoint: one decode helper and one error writer keep a whole API consistent
Form submissions from a React client that highlights each invalid field from the errors array
Public APIs where clients in other languages need a documented, machine-readable error format
Endpoints behind a proxy or gateway, where duplicate keys and case-folding would let two parsers disagree
strengths: Struct tags plus a decode helper replace a framework's binding layer; nothing is reflected that you can't see
Problem details is a standard format, so a client handles every error of every endpoint with one code path, unlike ad-hoc {"error": ...} bodies
MaxBytesReader and *MaxBytesError make the size limit a typed, testable error instead of a truncated body
Go 1.27's encoding/json/v2 rejects duplicate names, invalid UTF-8 and trailing data by default, without the wrapper code v1 needs
weaknesses: v1's defaults are lenient (unknown keys ignored, case-insensitive matching, duplicates accepted, invalid UTF-8 replaced) and each needs explicit handling
v1's unknown-field error has no exported type; you can only match its text (v2 has json.ErrUnknownName, and scrambles its message wording so nobody matches text)
No declarative validation in the standard library: unlike zod or Bean Validation, the rules are hand-written code (or a third-party validator)
A missing field and a zero value decode to the same thing; telling them apart needs pointer fields or json/v2's options

pitfalls.title: Reading an unbounded body
pitfalls.detail: json.NewDecoder(r.Body) reads as much as the client sends. Wrap the body in http.MaxBytesReader with a limit per endpoint.

pitfalls.title: Counting bytes instead of characters
pitfalls.detail: len(s) is bytes. A 20-character Turkish name can be 30 bytes. Use utf8.RuneCountInString for user-facing limits, and keep byte limits for storage and transport.

pitfalls.title: Echoing internal errors to clients
pitfalls.detail: err.Error() from encoding/json mentions Go struct and type names, and a database error can reveal table names. Map errors to client messages in one place and log the original.

pitfalls.title: Validating before decoding finished
pitfalls.detail: Validate the decoded struct, not the raw map. And remember that a body of null decodes without error, so required-field checks belong in validation, not in the decoder.

pitfalls.title: Choosing the status by habit
pitfalls.detail: 400 for bodies you can't parse, 413 for bodies over the limit, 415 for a wrong Content-Type, 422 for well-formed bodies that break the rules. The problem's status member must match the real response status.

quiz.q: A client sends {"name":"Ayşe"} {"name":"Eve"} to a handler that calls dec.Decode(&in) once. What happens with plain encoding/json (v1)?
options: It fails with a syntax error
in.Name is "Ayşe" and the rest is ignored
It fails with an unknown field error
quiz.why: Decode reads one value from the stream and stops. Only a second Decode (expecting io.EOF), or v2's UnmarshalRead, detects the trailing value.

quiz.q: The body is well-formed JSON but the e-mail is invalid. Which status fits best?
quiz.why: The syntax was fine; the content breaks a rule. 400 is for bodies that can't be parsed at all.

quiz.q: What does v1 encoding/json do with {"name":"a","NAME":"b"} decoded into a struct with a `json:"name"` field?
quiz.why: v1 matches keys case-insensitively and lets a later duplicate overwrite an earlier one; DisallowUnknownFields doesn't help, because NAME is not unknown. v2 rejects this input.

quiz.q: Why should a client branch on the problem's type rather than its title?
options: type is the stable identifier; title and detail are human-readable text that may change or be translated
quiz.why: RFC 9457 makes type the primary identifier of the problem kind; title is a human-readable summary.

further_reading.title: package encoding/json: Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields and the v1/v2 differences

body:
## Concept

The edge of an HTTP service is where untrusted bytes become typed values. Three steps,
always in this order:

1. **Decode strictly.** Cap the body size, reject unknown fields, accept exactly one JSON
   value. A failure here is the client's syntax problem: 400, or 413 for size.
2. **Validate.** Check the rules the type system can't express: lengths in characters,
   formats, ranges, cross-field rules. Collect all failures. A failure here is 422.
3. **Answer machine-readably.** RFC 9457 "Problem Details for HTTP APIs" (it obsoletes RFC
   7807) defines a JSON object with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`,
   served as `application/problem+json`, plus any extension members you need, such as an
   `errors` array of JSON Pointers to the bad fields.

Below the edge, code works with values that are already valid. Services and repositories
don't re-check that an e-mail looks like one.

Go 1.27 ships `encoding/json/v2`. The v1 package is now implemented on top of it with
options that keep v1's historical behavior, and its documentation encourages new code to
use v2, whose defaults are the strict ones.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **TypeScript/zod**: `schema.safeParse(body)` decodes and validates in one declarative
  step. In Go, decoding is driven by struct tags and validation is ordinary code, usually a
  `validate()` method. More typing, nothing hidden (lesson ts.services.zod).
- **Java/Spring**: `@Valid @RequestBody` with Bean Validation annotations, and
  `ProblemDetail` (Spring 6) for RFC 7807/9457 responses. Go has no annotations; the
  handler calls the helpers explicitly.
- **Python/FastAPI/pydantic**: a model class validates on construction and FastAPI answers
  422 with a list of field errors automatically. In Go you build that response yourself,
  which also means you choose its format.
- **Jackson (Java)**: a plain `ObjectMapper` fails on unknown properties. v1
  `encoding/json` ignores them, and so does v2 unless you pass `RejectUnknownMembers(true)`.

## Design notes

Write the helpers once per service: a `decodeJSON` (size limit, unknown fields, single
value, error mapping), a `writeJSON` and a `writeProblem`. StackLab's backend has the last
one as `problem(w, status, detail)` in `server/internal/httpapi/router.go`, and its run
handler decodes with `MaxBytesReader` and `json.NewDecoder`, the v1 form of example 1.

For new code on Go 1.27, `json.UnmarshalRead(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, n), &v,
json.RejectUnknownMembers(true))` gives you the single-value check, duplicate-name
rejection, case-sensitive matching and UTF-8 validation without wrapper code. Moving an
existing API from v1 to v2 is a behavior change for clients, so test it against real
traffic first: a client that sends `"Email"` instead of `"email"` worked yesterday.

Keep validation next to the type it validates, as a method, and keep it free of HTTP: it
returns field errors, and the handler decides that they become a 422. The same method then
serves a CLI import or a queue consumer. Return all field errors at once; a form that
reveals one error per submit is a frustrating form. Finally, never put `err.Error()` from
a lower layer into `detail` unfiltered: log it, and send the client a message written for
the client.

expected.strict-decode:
valid   200 hello Ayşe (30)
typo    400 json: unknown field "agee"
type    400 age: got string, want int
two     400 body must hold a single JSON value
null    200 hello  (0)
too big 413 body exceeds 1024 bytes
expected.v1-vs-v2:
duplicate name
  v1 accepted: name="Mallory"
  v2 rejected: jsontext: duplicate object member name "name"
other case
  v1 accepted: name="Mallory"
  v2 rejected: unknown object member name at /NAME
Windows-1254 ş
  v1 accepted: name="Ay�e"
  v2 rejected: jsontext: invalid UTF-8 within "/name" after offset 11
trailing data
  v1 accepted: name="Ayşe"
  v2 rejected: jsontext: invalid character '{' after top-level value after offset 17
unknown member
  v1 rejected: json: unknown field "admin"
  v2 rejected: unknown object member name at /admin
